transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42m
Attendees: Lena Morales (Redwood AE), Connor Patel (Redwood SE), Ava Chen (CTO - Harbor Tech), Marcus Lowe (DevOps), Priya Singh (Security), Samir Rao (ML Eng)

Auto-generated Summary (may be imperfect):
Redwood walked through private deployment topology options. Harbor Tech is leaning toward private VPC deployment for compliance; concerns about peering, CIDR overlaps, cross-account routing, and regional availability were discussed. Action items captured.

[00:00] Lena Morales: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, from Redwood. I'm Lena, account exec, and with me is Connor, our solutions engineer. How's everybody doin'?
[00:08] Ava Chen: Hi Lena, thanks. Good. We have a few people from infra and security on the call.
[00:11] Marcus Lowe: Marcus here, DevOps. Quick note, we have tight CIDR ranges in our prod VPCs.
[00:15] Priya Singh: Priya, security. We want to understand auditability, key mgmt, and how data egress is controlled.
[00:20] Connor Patel: Awesome, thanks. Today we want to cover high-level deployment options — hosted, dedicated, private — but focus on private VPC: VPC peering, PrivateLink, transit gateway patterns, and region constraints. We'll also flag typical firewall/NACL needs.
[00:34] Samir Rao: Also interested in latency and filesystem — I mean KV cache behavior across AZs.
[00:40] Lena Morales: Great. Quick qual — can you share current scale and what you'd like to run? e.g., per-minute qps, token volumes, any batch workloads?
[00:50] Ava Chen: We're targeting two use cases: real-time chat assistant for customer support (~50 QPS peak), and batch reranking jobs overnight. Model sizes will be 7B and some 30B for rerank. We need predictable latency for the chat.
[01:05] Connor Patel: Ok good. For private deployments we typically provision dedicated GPU pools in your VPC or peered VPCs depending on topology. Two patterns: 1) VPC peering (cross-account peer) with private endpoints in your VPC pointing to Redwood service endpoints, or 2) AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints) using endpoint services. Each has tradeoffs on routing and CIDR overlap.
[01:25] Marcus Lowe: We use multiple accounts and a TGW. CIDRs are tight — 10.0.0.0/16 used across prod; overlap is a pain. Peering may be blocked if CIDR overlaps.
[01:35] Connor Patel: Yeah, peering requires non-overlapping CIDRs. PrivateLink can work across overlap since it's an ENI-based interface endpoint in your VPC, so that's often our recommendation for cross-account setups, esp if you use Transit Gateway. But PrivateLink has some limits around number of AZ endpoints and costs.
[01:55] Priya Singh: Can you confirm whether PrivateLink supports VPC endpoints in all regions? We have some data residency requirements in eu-west-1 and us-east-1.
[02:05] Connor Patel: We support Private deployments in multiple regions; availability varies by cloud region for certain GPU shapes but PrivateLink is generally available. We'll share exact regional support matrix.
[02:18] Ava Chen: What's the TLS/key flow? We need KMS integration and customer-managed keys.
[02:22] Connor Patel: On private deploy we support customer-managed CMKs for data at rest. The control plane is optional — in some setups you run a private control plane in your VPC. For traffic between your services and inference, we use mTLS and you can bring your certificates; audit logs are shipped to your S3 or logging endpoint per retention policy. Some customers want HSM-backed keys — we can integrate with customer KMS/HSM via IAM roles.
[02:44] Marcus Lowe: If we do PrivateLink, how does DNS work? We host a lot of internal DNS entries.
[02:48] Connor Patel: With interface endpoints, AWS creates a dedicated DNS name, and you can override in your resolver. We often provide guidance for conditional forwarders so internal names resolve correctly.
[02:58] Lena Morales: Quick interjection — some customers choose Dedicated (Redwood-managed GPUs in dedicated account) instead of Private because it avoids exposing endpoints into their VPCs; tradeoff is network egress and trust model. Any preference?
[03:12] Ava Chen: Our compliance requires data not to leave our VPC unless encrypted and auditable. We prefer Private so logs and traffic stay under our control.
[03:20] Marcus Lowe: Also prefer peering through TGW if possible because our infra team's tooling expects TGW routes.
[03:28] Connor Patel: Ok TGW pattern is common: we offer instructions for registering endpoint services behind TGW and black-box the model serving. Note TGW-based routing can introduce additional latency if it routes through extra hops; usually <5–10 ms but depends on AZ topology.
[03:44] Samir Rao: For our latency SLO 200 ms p95, do you see issues with TGW?
[03:49] Connor Patel: Typically no, for 7B models and proper GPU infra we meet that, but for 30B rerank it's higher. We do continuous batching, but on private infra we'll tune batching and sequence lengths. We should run a short benchmark during POC.
[04:05] Priya Singh: On auditing: are all inference requests logged with token-level metadata? We need provenance for outputs.
[04:12] Connor Patel: We provide request-level logs with token counts, latency, model version, and request hash. For private deploy we can ship logs to your S3 bucket or CloudWatch/Stackdriver depending on cloud. Retention is configurable.
[04:25] Marcus Lowe: Is there an option to keep KV cache strictly ephemeral to avoid PII?
[04:29] Connor Patel: Yes, KV cache is ephemeral by design; we can disable persistent caching or route cache to isolated subnets. We'll include config examples.
[04:38] Ava Chen: Networking — what ports and security groups?
[04:41] Connor Patel: We need outbound TLS (443) to endpoint IPs if using peering, or interface ENIs for PrivateLink. Security groups will allow inbound from your application subnets to the endpoint ENIs. We'll send a checklist with port lists — typically 443 and health-check ports if you opt in.
[04:58] Speaker 1: Sorry, slight noise, but are there any egress charges we should expect?
[05:02] Lena Morales: There can be egress costs depending on topology. PrivateLink often reduces cross-AZ egress compared to cross-account peering, but TGW/data transfer pricing depends on cloud. We'll provide an estimate.
[05:15] Priya Singh: SOC2 stuff — do you have ISO? We need to review attestation.
[05:19] Lena Morales: Redwood is SOC2 Type II and has an ISO 27001 roadmap. We'll attach certs and our security pack.
[05:26] Marcus Lowe: For our firewall team we need exact IP ranges to whitelist. Is that static?
[05:31] Connor Patel: For PrivateLink ENIs the IPs are in your subnets; for peering we will provide the Redwood side IPs, but often customers host Redwood serving inside a dedicated account so it's within your control. If you want static egress, consider deploying the service in your account (private deployment with nodes in your VPC), then you control IPs.
[05:52] Ava Chen: How long does a private deployment take to stand up? Weeks?
[05:56] Lena Morales: Typical lead time is 2–4 weeks for initial setup (networking & security review) and then 1–2 weeks for provisioning and smoke tests. If GPU availability in region is constrained it can stretch longer.
[06:09] Samir Rao: Region question — we have eu-west-1 for EU data, but also us-east-1 for US. Can we replicate across regions?
[06:18] Connor Patel: Yes, multi-region is supported. We recommend deploying dedicated serving in each region and using smart routing. But note model variant compatibility and GPU shape availability differ by region; we'll provide a matrix.
[06:31] Priya Singh: For SSO and RBAC integration?
[06:34] Lena Morales: We support SAML/SSO for console access and fine-grained RBAC. For private deploys we can integrate with your IDP via SAML and push audit logs to your SIEM.
[06:46] Marcus Lowe: Example topologies?
[06:48] Connor Patel: Quick sketch: A) Single-account private deployment: Redwood nodes run in your VPC, you control subnets and IPs. B) Cross-account via TGW: your app VPC routes to a central infra account where Redwood nodes are peered via TGW. C) PrivateLink: Redwood exposes endpoint service, you create interface endpoints in each app VPC. Each has different tradeoffs for management, CIDR overlap, and latency.
[07:12] Ava Chen: We need to keep control plane on-prem-ish. Is private control plane supported?
[07:16] Connor Patel: Yes, private control plane option exists. You can host the control plane in your network or we can deploy a customer-owned control plane in your account. This ensures metadata and provisioning requests never hit the public internet.
[07:28] Lena Morales: Any blockers from compliance perspective?
[07:31] Priya Singh: We need explicit details on log retention, encryption in transit and at rest, and key custody. Also want to see network diagrams for peering and PrivateLink.
[07:40] Lena Morales: We'll provide the security pack and a sample network diagram.
[07:44] Marcus Lowe: Is there an on-prem option? We have a few air-gapped environments.
[07:48] Connor Patel: We do offer on-prem packages for regulated customers; it's more involved — requires local infra provisioning and potentially on-site support. We'll discuss if needed later.
[08:00] Samir Rao: POC plan?
[08:02] Lena Morales: Proposed: short POC in your dev account — we stand up a small private deployment or PrivateLink endpoints, run benchmarks for 7B chat and 30B rerank, and validate latency and logs.
[08:13] Ava Chen: That sounds right. For POC we need clear success criteria: p95 latency under 200 ms for chat, logs delivered to S3 within X minutes, and no CIDR conflicts.
[08:25] Connor Patel: Noted — we'll include a test plan.
[08:29] Priya Singh: For security review we'll need redacted architecture and the SOC2 report.
[08:33] Lena Morales: We'll send both.
[08:36] Marcus Lowe: A couple of nitty gritty: do you require any special IAM roles in our account?
[08:40] Connor Patel: We usually ask for cross-account role for provisioning if you opt for Redwood-managed nodes in your account; otherwise we use endpoint services and your team manages ENIs. We'll include role templates.
[08:52] Speaker 1: Is there a way to restrict model sizes available in the environment? We so we don't accidentally spin up huge models.
[08:58] Connor Patel: Yes, RBAC and per-route model pinning controls restrict which models can be invoked. We'll show that in the console demo.
[09:07] Ava Chen: Alright, can you walk us through a specific PrivateLink flow?
[09:10] Connor Patel: Sure. (slight pause) So Redwood registers an endpoint service in our infra account; you create an interface endpoint in your VPC, accept the service. Traffic flows over the ENI; your security groups control access. DNS resolves to the endpoint IPs; we provide guidance on route53 / resolver config. For multi-account, we recommend a central account to hold the endpoint to simplify management.
[09:34] Marcus Lowe: Ok and how about latency again? ENI inside same AZ, pretty low. If your service endpoints are cross-AZ then TGW may route across AZs and increase latency.
[09:45] Connor Patel: Correct. We try to colocate endpoints in same AZs to minimize cross-AZ hops. If you choose dedicated nodes in your account you get the best predictability.
[09:55] (background chatter)
[10:05] Ava Chen: Quick question on pricing: private deployment up-front vs ongoing?
[10:09] Lena Morales: Private has a platform subscription plus infra costs — monthly reserved capacity pricing for dedicated GPUs and licensing/ops fee for on-prem/private control plane. We'll send a pricing sketch.
[10:19] Samir Rao: For the benchmark, can we also test quantized 4-bit models?
[10:23] Connor Patel: Yep, we'll include quantized variants; quantization profiles are part of Redwood Optimize.
[10:29] Priya Singh: On encryption, do you support customer-managed keys for transitive caches?
[10:33] Connor Patel: Caches are ephemeral but for persistent storage we can use CMKs. We'll document config options.
[10:38] Ava Chen: Any guidance on subnet sizing?
[10:41] Connor Patel: We'll include recommended subnet sizes per node count and AZ distribution, plus ENI quotas. Customers often underprovision IPs, so we suggest /24 per subnet for initial sizing.
[10:54] Marcus Lowe: We'll probably run POC in our dev account first. Once that's good, we'll expand to prod and maybe do TGW centralization.
[11:01] Lena Morales: Sounds good. We'll also attach sample network diagrams with each topology option.
[11:06] Connor Patel: Also note some customers use a hybrid approach — PrivateLink for app VPCs and a central dedicated pool in a single infra account for heavy batch jobs.
[11:17] Ava Chen: Useful. Are there log formats and example entries we can get?
[11:21] Lena Morales: We'll include example JSON logs with request metadata and token counts.
[11:26] (brief silence)
[11:32] Priya Singh: Regarding compliance, how long do you retain logs by default?
[11:35] Connor Patel: Default retention 90 days, configurable. For enterprise we can enable longer retention to meet audit needs.
[11:43] Samir Rao: Any support for private peering with on-prem via Direct Connect/ExpressRoute?
[11:47] Connor Patel: Yes, if you have Direct Connect or ExpressRoute into your cloud VPCs, PrivateLink or peering over that path is supported. We'll coordinate with your networking team.
[11:57] Marcus Lowe: Great. Quick recap of blockers: CIDR overlap and TGW routing policy — we need to verify those.
[12:06] Lena Morales: Action items recap coming in email. We'll send the security pack, sample network diagrams, and the POC test plan.
[12:12] Ava Chen: Timeline? We'd like to start POC by week of Mar 9.
[12:16] Lena Morales: We'll aim to have docs and pricing by Mar 6 so you can schedule infra work.
[12:21] (several confirmations)
[12:25] Connor Patel: Anything else on regulatory or region constraints?
[12:28] Priya Singh: None beyond eu-west-1 residency requirement for EU data. We'll send a short note about which datasets are EU-only.
[12:36] Lena Morales: Perfect. We'll close with next steps.
[12:39] (wrap-up chatter)
[41:30] Lena Morales: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the pack and propose a time for the infra deep-dive.

End of transcript.

Notes: Transcript has occasional mis-attributions and minor transcription errors (speaker labels like Speaker 1). References to product names may be slightly altered (e.g., "PrivateLink" sometimes transcribed as "private link").
